title: their / there / they're
wrong: **Their** are many reasons to cycle to school.
right: **There** are many reasons to cycle to school.
why: *There* introduces something that exists, *their* shows possession, and *they're* is short for *they are*.
viCue: *họ / có* — the three English words sound identical

title: its / it's
wrong: The city lost **it's** old trees.
right: The city lost **its** old trees.
why: The apostrophe in *it's* stands for the missing letter of *is*, never for possession.

title: affect / effect
wrong: The new rule will **effect** every class.
right: The new rule will **affect** every class.
why: *Affect* is the verb; *effect* is almost always the noun (*have an effect on*).

title: than / then
wrong: Huế is quieter **then** Đà Nẵng.
right: Huế is quieter **than** Đà Nẵng.
why: *Than* follows a comparative; *then* means *after that*.

title: advice / advise
wrong: She **adviced** me to apply early.
right: She **advised** me to apply early.
why: *Advice* is the uncountable noun; *advise* is the verb, so it takes -d in the past.

title: in / on / at with place
wrong: I waited **on** the bus stop **in** the corner of the street.
right: I waited **at** the bus stop **on** the corner of the street.
why: *At* for a point, *on* for a surface or a line, *in* for an enclosed space.

title: Past modal without *have*
wrong: The delay **might been** caused by the rain.
right: The delay **might have been** caused by the rain.
why: A past modal is modal + *have* + past participle.

title: Two modals in a row
wrong: We **will can** finish the report next week.
right: We **will be able to** finish the report next week.
why: English allows one modal per verb phrase; use a phrasal modal for the second idea.

title: *must* used as a past form
wrong: She **musted** leave early yesterday.
right: She **had to** leave early yesterday.
why: *must* has no past form; use *had to* for past obligation.

title: Passive *be* does not agree with the new subject
wrong: The results **has been** shown to the head teacher.
right: The results **have been** shown to the head teacher.
why: In a passive, *be* agrees with the subject, which is often plural after the change.

title: Base verb after *be* in a passive
wrong: The labels should **be print** before Friday.
right: The labels should **be printed** before Friday.
why: A passive always takes the past participle, never the base form.

title: *want / would like* + *that*-clause
wrong: My parents **want that I study** medicine.
right: My parents **want me to study** medicine.
why: *want* and *would like* take an object + infinitive, not a *that*-clause.

title: *be used to* + base verb
wrong: I **am used to get** up at five.
right: I **am used to getting** up at five.
why: The *to* in *be/get used to* is a preposition, so it takes *-ing*; *used to* + base verb is the different, past-habit pattern.

title: Plural verb with an academic uncountable noun
wrong: The research **are** limited and her advice **were** practical.
right: The research **is** limited and her advice **was** practical.
why: *research, advice, evidence, information* are uncountable, so they take a singular verb.

title: *Which* clause left as its own sentence
wrong: The bus was late. **Which made** us miss the first talk.
right: The bus was late, **which made** us miss the first talk.
why: A *which* clause commenting on a whole sentence stays attached to it with a comma; alone it is a fragment.
viCue: *điều đó / cái mà* started as a new sentence

title: Doubled possessive after *whose*
wrong: I have a friend **whose her father** runs a bakery.
right: I have a friend **whose father** runs a bakery.
why: *whose* already carries the possessive, so *her/his/their* repeats it.

title: *Despite / In spite of* + clause
wrong: **Despite the shop was small**, it sold everything we needed.
right: **Although the shop was small**, it sold everything we needed. / **Despite its small size**, it sold…
why: *despite* and *in spite of* are prepositions and take a noun or *-ing*; a clause needs *although*.

title: Double negative after *unless*
wrong: **Unless you don't book** early, the tickets will sell out.
right: **Unless you book** early, the tickets will sell out.
why: *unless* already means *if… not*, so a second negative reverses the meaning.

title: Demonstrative does not match the number of the noun
wrong: I bought **this two books** before **these trip**.
right: I bought **these two books** before **this trip**.
why: *this/that* go with singular nouns; *these/those* go with plural ones.

title: Possessive determiner and possessive pronoun swapped
wrong: This bag is not **my**. It is **hers bag**.
right: This bag is not **mine**. It is **her bag**.
why: *my, her, their* need a noun after them; *mine, hers, theirs* stand alone.

title: Run-on sentence with no mark between clauses
wrong: My uncle drives a lorry **he leaves** before dawn.
right: My uncle drives a lorry**, and he leaves** before dawn.
why: Two complete sentences need a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction.
viCue: Vietnamese can chain clauses with no mark

title: *used to* + past verb
wrong: I **used to played** badminton after school.
right: I **used to play** badminton after school.
why: *used to* is always followed by the base verb.

title: Double past marking after *did*
wrong: We **didn't knew** the answer.
right: We **didn't know** the answer.
why: After *did* or *didn't*, the main verb goes back to its base form.

title: *would* for a past state
wrong: My uncle **would have** a small restaurant near the market.
right: My uncle **used to have** a small restaurant near the market.
why: *would* only describes repeated past actions; states take *used to* or the simple past.

title: Future perfect with a base verb
wrong: I **will have finish** the report by June.
right: I **will have finished** the report by June.
why: After *have*, use the past participle.

title: *Since* + simple past for a period up to now
wrong: **Since 2019 the school opened** three new clubs.
right: **Since 2019 the school has opened** three new clubs.
why: A period that runs up to now takes the present perfect, not the simple past.

title: Gerund subject with a plural verb
wrong: **Learning two languages take** time and patience.
right: **Learning two languages takes** time and patience.
why: An *-ing* subject is singular, however many nouns follow it.

title: *neither … nor* agreement
wrong: Neither my father nor my uncle **drive** a car.
right: Neither my father nor my uncle **drives** a car.
why: With *either… or* and *neither… nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
